name: Back-of-the-Envelope Estimation
intent: Get a rough but useful answer for traffic, storage and bandwidth in a few minutes, by stating assumptions, rounding hard and checking the result against numbers you know.
scenario: A photo-sharing app expects 10 million daily users, each uploading 2 photos a day of about 500 KB after the app compresses them. Before anyone draws a diagram, the team needs to know how many uploads arrive per second, how much storage to plan for a year and how much network capacity the upload servers need. The quick answers are about 200 uploads a second on average, 600 at the peak, 3.65 PB of new photos in a year and 2.4 Gbps at the peak.
problem: Design choices change at about every factor of 10: a few hundred requests a second fit on a handful of ordinary servers, tens of thousands need a fleet, and a database that holds terabytes behaves differently from one that holds petabytes. You cannot measure a system that does not exist yet, and waiting for exact numbers means choosing the architecture blind. Guessing without arithmetic is just as risky, because mistakes of 1,000 times are easy to make with millions of users and bytes. An estimate that is right within a factor of 2 or 3 is usually enough to pick the right design, and it takes minutes.

howItWorks.title: Write the assumptions down as numbers with units
howItWorks.text: Start by asking what you are estimating (requests per second, storage per year, bandwidth) and list every input: 10 million daily users, 2 uploads each, 500 KB per photo, peak at 3 times the average, kept for 1 year. These inputs are guesses, so say so and write them down. When someone disagrees later, they can change one assumption and redo the arithmetic instead of arguing about the answer. Always carry the unit on every line: a missing 'KB' or 'million' is how 1,000-times errors happen.

howItWorks.title: Round hard and count in powers of ten
howItWorks.text: Keep one or two significant digits and do the arithmetic as powers of ten: 10 million times 2 is 2 times 10 to the 7th, which is 20 million. Memorise the sizes: 1 thousand is 10 to the 3rd, 1 million 10 to the 6th, 1 billion 10 to the 9th, 1 trillion 10 to the 12th. Computer storage steps by 1,000 (KB, MB, GB, TB, PB), and the binary powers are close to the same numbers: 2 to the 10th is 1,024 (about a thousand), 2 to the 20th about a million, 2 to the 30th about a billion, 2 to the 40th about a trillion. Using 1,000 instead of 1,024 is off by under 3% per step and about 10% by the time you reach terabytes, which is noise in an estimate.

howItWorks.title: Know the latency ladder
howItWorks.text: Each rung of the ladder is much slower than the one above it. Roughly: reading from memory takes about 100 nanoseconds, a random read from an SSD about 100 microseconds (1,000 times slower), a round trip between two machines in the same data centre about 0.5 milliseconds, a spinning hard disk seek about 10 milliseconds, and a round trip to another region from tens of milliseconds to 150 or more, because light in fibre covers about 200,000 km per second. These are orders of magnitude, not measurements, and real values vary by hardware and distance. They tell you why a cache in memory beats a database call, why a chain of 10 sequential cross-region calls can cost a second or more, and which rung a design touches on every request.

howItWorks.title: Turn users into requests per second
howItWorks.text: There are 86,400 seconds in a day. Use 100,000: it is easier to divide by, and the answers come out about 14% low, which does not change a design decision. So requests per second is requests per day divided by 100,000. Handy anchors: 1 million requests a day is about 10 a second, 100 million a day about 1,000 a second, 1 billion a day about 10,000 a second. In the example, 10 million users times 2 uploads is 20 million a day, divided by 100,000 is 200 uploads per second on average.

howItWorks.title: Average is not peak
howItWorks.text: Traffic is never flat. People sleep, work and watch events at the same hours, so the busiest moment is a multiple of the daily average. If the busiest hour carries 10 to 15% of the day's requests, that hour runs at 2.4 to 3.6 times the average (10% times 24 hours, 15% times 24 hours), so 2 to 4 is a reasonable first guess for a consumer app, while a launch, a sale or a viral post can be 10 times or more. Size the servers for the peak, not the average, and leave headroom beyond it. In the example, 200 per second on average and a factor of 3 gives 600 per second at the peak.

howItWorks.title: Storage per year, with copies
howItWorks.text: Storage is items per day times size per item times days kept. In the example, 20 million photos times 500 KB is 10 TB a day, and 10 TB times 365 is 3,650 TB, or 3.65 PB, in a year (rounded hard, 10 TB times 400 is 4 PB). That is the raw data. Real systems also keep copies for safety (3 copies of 3.65 PB is about 11 PB), indexes, thumbnails and backups, and the data keeps growing as the user base does, so say which of these your number includes.

howItWorks.title: Bandwidth: requests per second times size
howItWorks.text: Peak bandwidth is peak requests per second times the size of each request: 600 per second times 500 KB is 300,000 KB a second, or 300 MB/s. Files are measured in bytes but network links are rated in bits, and a byte is 8 bits, so multiply by 8: 300 MB/s is 2,400 Mbps, or 2.4 Gbps. Against a 10 Gbps link that is 24%, so the uploads fit. Estimate reads and writes separately: if each photo is viewed 100 times, the traffic going out is about 100 times the traffic coming in.

howItWorks.title: Sanity-check, then use the answer
howItWorks.text: Before you trust a number, ask whether it is plausible. Compare it with something you know (the world has about 8 billion people; a 10 Gbps link carries 1.25 GB/s), recompute it a second way, and re-read the units. Then say which decision the number drives: 600 uploads a second is easily spread over a few servers, but 3.65 PB a year calls for object storage that grows by adding machines, not one database server. If the choice would not change between 300 and 1,200 requests a second, the estimate is precise enough, so stop and move on.

pros: Takes minutes and needs no tools, so it works in a meeting, an interview or the first hour of a design
Shows which choices matter, because the design changes at about every factor of 10
Puts every assumption on the page, where others can challenge or correct it
Catches impossible or wildly expensive ideas before anything is built
Builds a feel for scale, so wrong numbers start to look wrong
cons: The answer is only as good as the assumptions, and early assumptions are guesses
Rounding and averages hide spikes, hot spots and long tails that matter in production
Leaves out overheads such as protocol headers, retries, replication, indexes and backups unless you add them
A neat-looking number invites false confidence and can anchor a team on a wrong figure
Does not replace load tests or real measurements once the system exists
whenToUse: The start of a design, to decide whether one server, a fleet or a sharded database is the right size of problem
System design interviews and design reviews, where the numbers justify the architecture
Early capacity and cost planning, such as how much storage or network to budget for a year
Checking whether a feature is plausible before spending weeks on it
Sanity-checking someone else's figures, or a dashboard that looks too good or too bad
whenNotToUse: A system already running: use real metrics and traffic history instead of guesses
Final capacity commitments, service level promises or large purchases: load test and add a safety margin
Finding a slow query, a hot key or tail latency: these need profiling and per-request data, not averages
Exact billing or financial forecasts, where a rough factor of 2 is not acceptable
Decisions the number cannot change: if every sensible estimate leads to the same design, skip the arithmetic
pitfalls: False precision: dividing by 86,400 and reporting 231.48 requests a second from guessed inputs; one or two significant digits is the honest precision
Sizing for the average instead of the peak, so the system works at 3 a.m. and falls over at 8 p.m.
Mixing bits and bytes: 300 MB/s is 2.4 Gbps, and treating them as equal makes the bandwidth answer 8 times too small
Dropping a unit or a factor of 1,000 (KB for MB, millions for billions) because the units were not written on each line
Estimating writes only, when reads are often 10 to 100 times more numerous and drive the cache, database and egress costs
Forgetting copies, indexes, thumbnails and backups, so raw storage is quoted as if it were the amount to buy
Hiding assumptions ('lots of users') so nobody can challenge them, or never saying which ones you are least sure of
Skipping the sanity check, and sending a result such as 5 PB a day from a small start-up straight into a design

roles.description: Writes the assumptions, rounds hard and does the arithmetic on paper.

quiz.question: A chat app has 50 million daily users who each send 4 messages a day. Using 100,000 as the number of seconds in a day, about how many messages per second is that on average?
quiz.explanation: 50 million times 4 is 200 million messages a day, which is 2 times 10 to the 8th. Dividing by 10 to the 5th (100,000) leaves 2 times 10 to the 3rd, or about 2,000 a second. About 20,000 divides by 10,000 by mistake, and about 200,000 divides by only 1,000. About 200 loses a factor of 10 early, as if there were 5 million users, not 50 million.

quiz.question: At its busiest moment a service must send 20 MB per second. Its network link is rated at 100 Mbps. Is one link enough?
options: Yes, because 20 is well below 100, so there is plenty of room
No, because 20 MB/s is 160 Mbps, which is above 100 Mbps
Yes, because a 100 Mbps link carries 100 MB each second
No, because 20 MB/s is 2,000 Mbps, so it needs 20 links
quiz.explanation: File sizes are in bytes and links are rated in bits, and a byte is 8 bits, so 20 MB/s is 160 Mbps and one 100 Mbps link is not enough. Comparing 20 with 100 ignores the 8 times difference in units, and the same slip explains the claim that the link carries 100 MB each second (it carries about 12.5 MB each second). The last answer multiplies by 100 instead of 8; 2,000 Mbps would be 250 MB/s.

quiz.question: A teammate says an app will write 500 GB of new data a day and so needs about 5 TB of storage for one year of data. How do you respond?
options: Nothing is wrong, since a year of storage is about ten times the daily amount
It is only low because backups are missing, so 5 TB is otherwise about right
It is too high, because data written long ago is always deleted soon after
It is far too low: 500 GB a day is about 180 TB in a year
quiz.explanation: Storage per year is the daily amount times about 365 (or 400 when rounded hard): 500 GB times 365 is about 182 TB, around 36 times the claim, and copies and backups would add more. A year is not ten days of data, so the first answer is wrong. Missing backups cannot explain a 36-times gap, and deleting old data is a retention decision that has to be stated as an assumption, not something that happens by itself.
